title: The Land of the Light Spiritual

chapters.title: Landfall at Colombo
chapters.src: First Public Lecture in the East (Colombo)
lines: On the afternoon of the fifteenth of January, eighteen ninety-seven, Swami Vivekananda lands at Colombo.
He is coming home, after his work in the West.
From here the road will run north: to Jaffna, across to Pamban and Rameswaram, up through Madura and Madras.
Then to Calcutta, and on to the Himalayas at Almora.
Twenty-nine talks lie along that road. This is the first.

chapters.title: The welcome
chapters.src: First Public Lecture in the East (Colombo)
lines: The Hindus of Colombo give him a right royal reception, and read an address of welcome.
It thanks him for proclaiming to Europe and America the Hindu ideal of a universal religion, harmonising all creeds.
In his brief reply, he points out whom they have come out to honour.
Not a great politician, not a great soldier, not a millionaire, but a begging Sannyasin.
Religion, he urges, must stay the backbone of the national life, if the nation is to live.
The next evening, the sixteenth, he speaks in the Floral Hall.

chapters.title: Punya Bhumi
chapters.src: First Public Lecture in the East (Colombo)
lines: He begins by giving the credit away: whatever he did in the West came from the blessings that followed him from home.
What had been an emotional belief, he says, has gained the certainty of conviction.
Every Hindu calls this land the Punya Bhumi, the land of Karma.

lines.q: Today I stand here and say, with the conviction of truth, that it is so.

lines: If any land is the one to which every soul wending its way Godward must come, to attain its last home,

lines.q: the land of introspection and of spirituality — it is India.

lines: From here, tidal waves of philosophy have covered the earth. From here must start the wave that will spiritualise the material civilisation of the world.

chapters.title: Blood or blessing
chapters.src: First Public Lecture in the East (Colombo)
lines: The debt the world owes to the patient Hindu, the mild Hindu, is immense.
Elsewhere, great ideas travelled with the blast of war trumpets and the march of embattled cohorts.

lines.q: Each idea had to be soaked in a deluge of blood.

lines: Each word of power was followed by the wails of orphans, and the tears of widows.
From India, idea after idea has marched out, every word spoken with a blessing behind it and peace before it.

lines.q: We, of all nations of the world, have never been a conquering race, and that blessing is on our head, and therefore we live.

chapters.title: A spider's web on the Capitol
chapters.src: First Public Lecture in the East (Colombo)
lines: There was a time when the earth trembled at the march of big Greek battalions. That ancient land is gone.
There was a time when the Roman Eagle floated over everything worth having in this world.

lines.q: But the Capitoline Hill is a mass of ruins, the spider weaves its web where the Caesars ruled.

lines: Other glorious nations came and went, vanishing like ripples on the face of the waters.
But we live. If Manu came back today, he would not find himself in a foreign land.
Blow after blow of misfortune has only made the old laws stronger. The mainspring of the national life, he says, is here.

chapters.title: The ploughman's mark
chapters.src: First Public Lecture in the East (Colombo)
lines: To other nations, religion is one occupation among many: politics, society, wealth, the senses, and perhaps a little bit of religion.
Here, in India, religion is the one and the only occupation of life.
Few here have heard of the Sino-Japanese War. Yet even the poorest labourer knows there was a Parliament of Religions in America, and a Hindu Sannyasin sent there.
Ask a ploughman in England or America his politics, and he names his party; he even knows something about the silver question.
Ask his religion: he goes to church, belongs to a denomination, and that is all he knows.
Ask an Indian ploughman about politics, and he says, what is that? Ask his religion, and he says:

lines.q: Look here, my friend, I have marked it on my forehead.

lines: That is our nation's life.

chapters.title: Storing the light
chapters.src: First Public Lecture in the East (Colombo)
lines: Each man comes into the world with a bent, marked out by his past Karma. And what is true of the individual is true of the race.

lines.q: Political greatness or military power is never the mission of our race; it never was, and, mark my words, it never will be.

lines: Its mission is to conserve, to accumulate, as it were into a dynamo, all the spiritual energy of the race,
and to pour it forth in a deluge on the world, whenever circumstances are propitious.
Let the Persian, the Greek, the Roman, the Arab or the Englishman march his battalions and link the nations; India's thought flows along the new-made channels.

lines.q: India's gift to the world is the light spiritual.

chapters.title: Like the gentle dew
chapters.src: First Public Lecture in the East (Colombo)
lines: Whenever a conquering nation linked India to the world, the world was flooded with Indian spiritual ideas.
At the beginning of this century, Schopenhauer studied the Upanishads in a Latin translation of an old Persian one, and wrote:
In the whole world there is no study so beneficial and so elevating as that of the Upanishads. It has been the solace of my life, it will be the solace of my death.

lines.q: We never preached our thoughts with fire and sword.

lines: If one English word names India's gift, it is fascination: a charm that comes imperceptibly, to those who persevere.

lines.q: Slow and silent, as the gentle dew that falls in the morning, unseen and unheard yet producing a most tremendous result,

lines: has been the work of the calm, patient, all-suffering spiritual race upon the world of thought.

chapters.title: Porcelain cracks
chapters.src: First Public Lecture in the East (Colombo)
lines: Once more, history is going to repeat itself.
Under the blasting light of modern science, old and apparently invulnerable beliefs have been shattered to their very foundations.
Antiquarian research pulverises antiquated orthodoxies, like masses of porcelain.
The old sects looked upon the world as a little mud-puddle, and thought that time began but the other day.
Evolution and the conservation of energy are dealing death blows to crude theologies.
What can hold cultured humanity now? The Vedanta: the oneness of all, the eternal soul of man, the infinite range of time, space, and causation.

chapters.title: Shruti and Smriti
chapters.src: First Public Lecture in the East (Colombo)
lines: But what goes out to the world is only the principles, the foundation; not the details of custom.
Our books make a clear distinction between two sets of truths.
One set abides for ever: the nature of the soul, of God, of perfection; creation, or more correctly speaking, projection; the law of cyclical procession.
These are founded upon universal laws in nature, and belong to the Shrutis.
The other set, the minor laws of everyday life, belongs to the Puranas and the Smritis.
Customs of one Yuga are not the customs of another. Great Rishis will appear, and lead us to customs suited to new environments.

chapters.title: Gods of the tribes
chapters.src: First Public Lecture in the East (Colombo)
lines: Watch religions grow, and you find each tribe begins with a god of its own.
Allied Babylonian tribes called their gods Baal. The Jewish tribes called theirs Moloch.
Then one tribe rises over the rest, and its god must become the god of all.
Baal-Merodach, said the Babylonians, was the greatest. Moloch-Yahveh was over all the other Molochs.
These questions had to be decided by the fortunes of battle.
In India too, competing gods struggled with each other for supremacy.

chapters.title: Ekam sat
chapters.src: First Public Lecture in the East (Colombo)
lines: But in the midst of the din and confusion, there came a voice.

lines.q: Ekam sad vipra bahudha vadanti. That which exists is One; sages call It by various names.

lines: Not that Shiva is superior to Vishnu: it is the same One, whom you call by a hundred other names.

lines.q: The whole history of India you may read in these few words.

lines: It was repeated till it tingled in every drop of the nation's blood, and the land became the most wonderful land of toleration.
So a dualist and a monist, the eternal servant of God and the one who is one with God, are both good Hindus.

chapters.title: Rivers to one ocean
chapters.src: First Public Lecture in the East (Colombo)
lines: Elsewhere he has seen tremendous religious persecution, in every country he has been.

lines.q: It is here that Indians build temples for Mohammedans and Christians; nowhere else.

lines: The Mahimnah-stotra says: as the different rivers, taking their start from different mountains, running straight or crooked, at last come unto the ocean,
so, O Shiva, the different paths which men take, crooked or straight, all lead unto Thee.
A real lover of Shiva sees Him not only in the Linga, but in everything and in everyone.
Knees bending towards the Caaba, kneeling in a Christian church, or in a Buddhist temple, all are kneeling to Him, whether they know it or not.

chapters.title: Not toleration, sympathy
chapters.src: First Public Lecture in the East (Colombo)
lines: Difference cannot cease; without variation life must cease. But it is not necessary that we should hate each other.

lines.q: The one great lesson, therefore, that the world wants most, that the world has yet to learn from India, is the idea not only of toleration, but of sympathy.

lines: Mildness, gentleness, forbearance, toleration, sympathy, and brotherhood: everyone may learn them, man, woman, or child, without respect of race, caste, or creed.

lines.q: They call Thee by various names; Thou art One.

lines: From Colombo, the road runs north, to Jaffna.
